title: React Context & State Management: A Field Handbook
summary: A dense, practical tour of React's Context API — how useContext subscribes, why providers cause re-renders, and how to split contexts, apply useReducer, and know when a local context stops being enough. Covers mechanics, cost models, patterns, comparisons with external stores, and the mistakes that bite in real apps.

chapters.title: Why Context Exists: Prop Drilling & the Problem Space
points: Prop drilling defined: passing a value through components that don't use it, only to reach a deep consumer
Concrete example: `<App>` holds `theme`, passes it through `Layout` → `Sidebar` → `NavItem`; two middle components touch a prop they never read
Cost of drilling: every intermediate component's props signature couples to a value it doesn't own, so refactors ripple
Context is a transport mechanism, not a state manager — it moves a value down the tree without touching intermediate props
Key distinction: Context solves *distribution*, `useState`/`useReducer` solve *storage*. Most confusion comes from conflating the two
Composition as the alternative React docs recommend first: pass JSX as `children` so the deep component is created where the data lives
Example: `<Layout sidebar={<NavItem theme={theme} />} />` eliminates the drill without any context
When drilling is fine: 1–2 levels, stable value, small tree. Context adds indirection that hurts readability if used too eagerly
Historical note: Context was an unstable/legacy API before React 16.3; the modern `createContext` API is the only supported one
Rule of thumb: reach for Context when a value is genuinely 'ambient' — theme, locale, auth user, router state — not for every shared value

chapters.title: The Core API: createContext, Provider, useContext
points: `const ThemeContext = createContext(defaultValue)` creates a context object with a `.Provider` (and legacy `.Consumer`)
The default value is used only when a component reads the context with NO matching Provider above it — not when the Provider passes `undefined`
Provider usage: `<ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>`
React 19: the context object itself is renderable as a provider — `<ThemeContext value={theme}>` — the `.Provider` suffix is deprecated
`const theme = useContext(ThemeContext)` reads the value from the *nearest* Provider above in the tree
React 19 adds `use(ThemeContext)` which can be called conditionally, unlike `useContext` which obeys the rules of Hooks
Nesting overrides: an inner Provider shadows an outer one for its subtree — this powers nested themes and per-route overrides
The `undefined` default trap plus the guard hook pattern: `if (ctx === undefined) throw new Error('useTheme must be used within ThemeProvider')`
Typed custom hook example: `export function useTheme() { const c = useContext(ThemeContext); if (!c) throw new Error(...); return c }` — export the hook, not the raw context
Class-era `Context.Consumer` render-prop form still works and is the only option inside class components
Context is per-React-tree, not global: two separate roots have independent Provider chains
Importing the context object from two different module instances (duplicate bundle copies) creates two distinct contexts — a real cause of 'default value' bugs

chapters.title: Mechanics: How a Context Read Actually Propagates
points: Each context object holds a `_currentValue` slot that React writes when a Provider renders and restores when it pops
`useContext` does two things: reads `_currentValue`, and registers the calling fiber as a dependency on that context
Dependencies are stored on the fiber as a linked list of context items, alongside the hook chain
On Provider re-render React compares old vs new `value` with `Object.is`; if equal, it can bail out of propagation entirely
If the value changed, React walks the Provider's subtree looking for fibers that read this context and schedules an update on each
This propagation is why context updates reach consumers even through components that returned `React.memo`-bailed-out subtrees
Memo is NOT a barrier for context: `memo` blocks prop-driven re-renders, but a context read punches straight through
The consumer re-renders regardless of which *part* of the value changed — there is no field-level subscription
Reading context is a subscription; passing the same value down as a prop is not — the update mechanisms are different
Context updates participate in normal React scheduling: they can be batched, transitioned via `startTransition`, and interrupted in concurrent rendering
Consequence to memorize: re-renders from context are driven by *identity of the value*, and *nothing else*

chapters.title: The Provider Re-Render Cost Model
points: Two independent causes of consumer re-renders: (1) the context value's identity changed, (2) the Provider's parent re-rendered and re-rendered `children` as ordinary elements
Cause 2 explained: if `<Provider>{<App/>}</Provider>` lives inside a component that re-renders, `App` re-renders as a child — not because of context at all
The `children` fix: put state in a component that takes `children` as a prop, so `children` keeps a stable element identity and React skips re-rendering it
Code: `function ThemeProvider({children}) { const [t, setT] = useState(); const v = useMemo(() => ({t, setT}), [t]); return <Ctx value={v}>{children}</Ctx> }`
The object-literal trap: `value={{ user, setUser }}` creates a new object every render, so `Object.is` always fails and every consumer re-renders
Fix with `useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user])` — setters from `useState`/`useReducer` are already stable, so they need not be dependencies
Functions in the value need `useCallback` or to be defined outside render, or the memo is defeated by an unstable function identity
Cost formula intuition: cost ≈ (number of consumers in subtree) × (render cost of each) × (update frequency of the value)
A high-frequency value (mouse position, form input, timer tick) with many consumers is the pathological case — this is where context earns its bad reputation
Consumers that render trivial output are cheap; the real cost is a consumer whose subtree is a large uncontrolled render
`React.memo` on the *children of* a consumer limits blast radius: the consumer re-renders, but its memoized children don't if props are stable
Measure before optimizing: React DevTools Profiler with 'Record why each component rendered' names context as the trigger explicitly

chapters.title: Splitting Contexts: The Highest-Leverage Fix
points: Principle: separate values that change at different rates into separate contexts, so each consumer subscribes to the smallest thing it needs
The canonical split: state context vs. dispatch/actions context — the dispatch function never changes identity, so action-only consumers never re-render
Example: `<StateCtx value={state}><DispatchCtx value={dispatch}>{children}</DispatchCtx></StateCtx>` with `useTodos()` and `useTodosDispatch()` hooks
A button that only calls `dispatch({type:'add'})` reads only the dispatch context and is immune to every state change
Second split axis: by domain — `AuthContext`, `ThemeContext`, `CartContext` rather than one `AppContext` holding everything
Third split axis: by volatility — put a fast-changing field (draft input text) in its own context away from slow-changing config
Provider nesting order matters for readability, not correctness; a `composeProviders` helper flattens deep pyramid nesting
Trade-off: more contexts = more providers, more files, more indirection. Split when profiling shows a cost, or when the volatility difference is obvious up front
Anti-pattern: one god context whose value is `{...everything}` — every consumer becomes coupled to every state change in the app
`useMemo` per-context still applies: each split context's value needs its own stable identity
Selector-in-userland attempt: `useContextSelector` is a userland library (`use-context-selector`), NOT built into React — it works by bypassing the context propagation with its own subscription
React's own `useSyncExternalStore` is the sanctioned escape hatch for selector-style subscriptions when splitting isn't enough

chapters.title: useReducer: Structuring the State Itself
points: Signature: `const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialArg, init?)` — the third arg lazily computes initial state via `init(initialArg)`
Reducer contract: `(state, action) => newState`, must be pure, must not mutate `state`, must return a new object for changes to be seen
`dispatch` has a stable identity for the lifetime of the component — safe to omit from dependency arrays and safe to put in context
Example reducer with a discriminated union of actions: `{type:'add', text}`, `{type:'toggle', id}`, `{type:'delete', id}` and a `default: throw new Error('unknown action ' + action.type)`
When useReducer beats useState: multiple pieces of state that update together, next state depends on previous, or update logic is complex enough to test in isolation
Testability: a reducer is a plain function, testable without rendering — `expect(reducer(state, {type:'add'})).toEqual(...)`
React may call the reducer twice in development StrictMode to surface impurity — this is a detection tool, not a bug
Dispatching during render is only legal for the *same* component's own state (render-phase update); anything else must be in an event handler or effect
Bailout rule: if the reducer returns the exact same state object (`Object.is` equal), React bails out and may skip re-rendering the subtree
`useState` is literally implemented on the same machinery as `useReducer` with a built-in basic state reducer
Combining with context: `useReducer` in the provider + split state/dispatch contexts is the standard 'Redux without Redux' pattern
Limitation: `useReducer` has no built-in async — side effects go in the calling code, in effects, or in an action-creator layer you write yourself

chapters.title: Patterns That Work in Real Apps
points: The provider module pattern: one file exports `XProvider`, `useX`, `useXDispatch`, and keeps the context object private
Guard hook so a missing provider fails loudly at the call site instead of silently yielding `undefined`
The `children`-stable provider so the provider's own state changes don't force the whole subtree to re-render
Reducer + context + async: expose action functions (`login`, `logout`) from a memoized object rather than exposing raw `dispatch` when actions need to await
Ref-in-context escape hatch: store a fast-changing value in a `useRef` inside the provider and expose a subscribe function, so reads don't trigger renders
Server Components caveat: `createContext` and Providers are client-only — a provider file needs `'use client'`, and RSC data should be passed as props
Initialization from props: `<ThemeProvider initial={serverTheme}>` lets a server-rendered value seed client state without a flash
Per-route / per-feature providers mounted low in the tree instead of one global provider at the root — smaller subtree = smaller blast radius
Multiple instances of the same provider for scoped state, e.g. a `FormProvider` per form rather than one global form context
Testing: wrap components in the real provider in tests rather than mocking the context — it exercises the actual reducer
Devtools naming: `ThemeContext.displayName = 'Theme'` makes the Profiler and component tree readable
Context + `useSyncExternalStore`: put an immutable store *object* in context (never changes identity) and let each consumer subscribe with its own selector

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Their Symptoms
points: Inline object value — `value={{a, b}}` — causes every consumer to re-render on every provider render. Symptom: Profiler shows unrelated components flashing
Forgetting `useCallback` on functions inside a memoized value, so the `useMemo` produces a new object anyway
Putting a high-frequency value (input text, scroll position, timer) into a widely-consumed context — symptom: typing lag
One god context: every feature re-renders when any feature changes; symptom is re-render counts that scale with app size, not with the change
Assuming `React.memo` protects against context updates — it does not; a context read bypasses memo entirely
Missing provider producing the default value silently — a `null`/`undefined` default plus a throwing hook catches this at once
Duplicate context objects from two module copies (monorepo, mismatched peer deps) — consumers read the default despite a Provider being visibly present
Using context for server data that should be cached/refetched — leads to hand-rolled caching, staleness bugs, and no request dedupe
Mutating state inside a reducer (`state.items.push(x); return state`) — React bails out on the identical reference and the UI doesn't update
Calling `useContext` conditionally — breaks the rules of Hooks; use React 19's `use()` if a conditional read is genuinely needed
Deriving expensive values in every consumer instead of once in the provider — duplicated computation across the whole subtree
Over-splitting too early: five contexts for values that all change together adds ceremony with zero re-render benefit

chapters.title: Context vs External Stores: The Comparison Table
points: Subscription granularity — Context: whole-value, all consumers; Redux/Zustand/Jotai: per-selector, only components whose slice changed
Re-render on unrelated change — Context: yes; external store with selectors: no
Bundle cost — Context: 0 KB (built in); Zustand ≈1 KB; Jotai ≈3 KB; Redux Toolkit ≈12 KB+ gzipped (approximate, check current sizes)
Read outside React — Context: impossible; external stores: `store.getState()` works from anywhere, including non-React code
DevTools & time travel — Context: none beyond the Profiler; Redux: full action log, time-travel, replay
Middleware / side effects — Context: hand-rolled; Redux: middleware pipeline, thunks, sagas, RTK listeners
Server-state features (caching, dedupe, revalidation, retries) — Context: none; TanStack Query / SWR: all of it
Boilerplate — Context+useReducer: moderate; Zustand: minimal; Redux Toolkit: moderate with strong conventions
Learning cost and team ceiling — Context is React-native knowledge; a store is one more mental model, but a standardized one
Persistence / hydration — Context: manual; stores: middleware for localStorage, URL, and SSR hydration
Concurrent-safe reads — external stores must use `useSyncExternalStore` to avoid tearing; Context is tear-free by construction
The honest summary row: Context wins on zero-dependency ambient values; stores win on frequent updates, selective reads, and tooling

chapters.title: When to Reach for an External Store
points: Signal 1: profiling shows re-renders driven by fields a component doesn't read, and splitting contexts has stopped helping
Signal 2: updates are frequent (many per second) and consumers are numerous — cursor position, live collaboration, animation state
Signal 3: you need to read or write state outside the React tree — an event listener, a websocket handler, an imperative library callback
Signal 4: server data — if the state is a cache of something remote, use TanStack Query or SWR, not Context and not Redux
Signal 5: you're rebuilding middleware — you've hand-written undo/redo, persistence, or an action log on top of your reducer
Signal 6: the provider pyramid has grown past ~6 levels and composition helpers are papering over an architecture problem

Picking one: Zustand for a small hook-shaped store with selectors; Jotai/Recoil for atomic, bottom-up derived state; Redux Toolkit for large teams needing conventions and devtools; XState when the logic is a real state machine
The middle option people forget: keep Context, but put an immutable store object in it and subscribe with `useSyncExternalStore` — you get selectors without a dependency
`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` — the third argument is required for SSR or hydration will mismatch
Counter-signal — do NOT migrate for: theme, locale, auth user, feature flags, or anything that changes a handful of times per session
Counter-signal: 'the app is getting bigger' alone is not a reason; the reason must be a measured re-render cost or a capability Context can't provide
Migration path is incremental: contexts and stores coexist; move one high-churn domain at a time and keep the ambient ones in Context

chapters.title: Decision Guide & Summary
points: Decision ladder: local `useState` → lift state up → composition/`children` → Context → Context + `useReducer` → split contexts → external store
Take each rung only when the one below it demonstrably fails; skipping rungs is how apps acquire Redux for a theme toggle
`useState` vs `useReducer`: independent simple values → state; several values that move together or complex transitions → reducer
Context is distribution, not storage — remember that and half the confusion disappears
The three optimizations, in order of leverage: stable value identity (`useMemo`), stable `children`, split contexts
Provider re-render checklist: is the value memoized? are functions stable? does the provider take `children`? is the value split by change rate?
Never assume — profile. React DevTools 'why did this render' names the context that triggered the update
Server state ≠ client state. Cache-shaped data belongs in a query library regardless of how you manage the rest
Context's real strengths: zero bundle cost, no tearing, scoped and nestable, works with Suspense and transitions
Context's real limits: no selectors, no external reads, no devtools, cost scales with consumer count
One-line mental model: a Provider is a broadcast — everyone in the subtree who tuned in hears every message, so keep the messages rare or the audience small
Final rule: optimize for the reader first, the profiler second, and reach for a store only when the profiler insists
